https://nineoclock.ro/romanian-language-.text: ABOUT US NINE O’CLOCK STAFF 2024 COMMERCIAL OFFER – 2026 Subscribe to the Nine O’Clock 2026 CONTACT Special price offer 2026 with a 50% discount August 31 marks Romanian Language Day, a celebration of one of the defining elements of Romania’s national identity and a living expression of the country’s history, culture and spirituality. For millions of people around the world, Romanian is far more than a means of communication. It is the language of family, memory and belonging — a connection to their roots and to the country’s rich cultural heritage. “President Dan: Today we celebrate Romanian Language Day at a particularly significant moment: for the first time, we are celebrating it together in three countries – Romania, the Republic of Moldova and Ukraine. Protecting the rights of Romanians abroad and promoting our language and culture remain key objectives of the Romanian state beyond its borders.We are united by this valuable bond of the Romanian language, which anchors us in history and opens the way to the future.Long live the Romanian language, and happy Romanian Language Day to all those who speak it, write it and keep it alive!’ “ Romanian is spoken as a mother tongue by more than 30 million people worldwide, with a significant part of the Romanian-speaking community living outside the country. Over the past decades, the growing presence of Romanians abroad has given the language a new dynamism, making it increasingly visible in some of Europe’s largest and most multicultural cities. From London to Madrid, Rome, Paris and beyond, Romanian can be heard in homes, schools, churches, universities and workplaces. Romanians who live, work, study or travel abroad are not only part of the communities in which they have settled, but also informal ambassadors of their language and culture. In the United Kingdom, for example, cultural and social initiatives organised by the Romanian Embassy in London, together with the Romanian Cultural Institute and Romanian organisations and associations from the diaspora, contribute to preserving and promoting Romanian language and culture. Such initiatives create opportunities for Romanian communities to celebrate their heritage while sharing it with the wider society. Romanian schools abroad have a particularly important role in this process. So do churches, cultural institutions and Romanian-language media. Together, they help ensure that the language continues to be spoken and passed on from one generation to the next. For Romanians living abroad, their mother tongue represents a precious legacy: their roots, their connection with home and a link with a history stretching back centuries. For children born and raised outside Romania, learning Romanian can become an important part of understanding their family heritage and identity. Keeping the language alive across generations is therefore both a personal and a collective responsibility. It is a way of honouring the past while investing in the future. Romanian Language Day is also an opportunity to reflect on the beauty and richness of the language itself. Romanian literature and poetry have repeatedly celebrated the power of words to preserve memory, express emotion and connect generations. As a well. Did you know? The Romanian Language Day is observed on the 31st of August. The language is spoken by approximately 25 million people worldwide It is the official language of both Romania and Moldova, where it is also known as Moldovan. https://www.dw.com/en/czech-pm-andrej-ba.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NCRe Babis announced on Monday that the Czech state will run a deficit of 386 billion crowns (€15.8 billion or $18 billion) next year Image: Michaela Rihova/CTK/picture alliance Advertisement The Czech Republic "must remain committed to increasing defense spending," Matthew Whitaker, the US envoy to NATO , demanded in Prague last week. "We ⁠expect our allies to step up," he said. The call is nothing new. As warnings about the threat emanating from Russia increase, and Washington demands European allies take greater responsibility for security, NATO has raised its target for defense spending from 2% to 3.5% of GDP, and pressure on those lagging is rising. Czechia, alongside Slovenia and Albania , has yet to meet the old target. But Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis , whose government cut the defense budget for 2026 to around 1.7% of GDP when it took office late last year, pushed back against the latest barb from Washington. While reiterating that NATO membership is crucial for Czechia, the premier bluntly stated that the government cannot afford to accelerate spending. He has pledged to hit the 2% target in 2027 but plans no further increases. US Ambassador to NATO Matthew G. Whitaker (pictured here in Iowa earlier this month) has made the US position clear to Prague: Czechia 'must remain committed to increasing defense spending' Image: Tim Evans/REUTERS That leaves the populist billionaire hoping that a personal rapport with US President Donald Trump will protect the country amid the burgeoning row. Warnings of a growing threat Whether Trump will protect Czechia from the threat of Russian hybrid warfare targeting Central European NATO allies is another question. A growing wave of stray drones and Russian intelligence operations — suspected bombings, sabotage and cyber warfare — have spread alarm in the neighborhood. Germany and Poland — key Czech partners — have reported high-profile incidents and linked them to attempts to intimidate Ukrainian allies. Czechia should understand the threat better than most, having been among the first to experience such an attack. Czechia's Security Information Service (BIS) reported in 2021 that the bombing of a depot storing weapons linked to Ukraine seven years previously had been carried out by Russia's domestic intelligence agency, the Federal Security Service (FSB). Babis, then in his first stint as PM, responded by expelling around 100 Russian diplomats and embassy staff, freezing relations with Moscow. The BIS remains in step with other intelligence agencies across the region in warning that the threat from Russia is growing. However, like its predecessors, the Babis government has failed to keep pace in terms of the national defense budget, even as neighbors have leapt into action. Prague spent just 1.86% of GDP on defense last year; Poland and the Baltic States have already met the new NATO target and will hit 5% next year. Prague's priorities Babis has made it clear this approach will not change. However, his claim that Czechia can't afford to boost defense spending is at odds with the 2027 budget his government approved on September 22. The fiscal plan will expand expenditure generously and targets Czechia's second-highest deficit ever at 386 billion Czech crowns (€15.8 billion or $18 billion). While finally catching up to the old NATO target will account for some of that spending, most of the increased outlay will reflect the coalition government's domestic political priorities. The plan clearly reflects the election campaign promises of Babis's ANO party and its junior partners, the far-right Freedom and Direct Democracy party (SPD) and radical-right Motorists for Themselves party. They all say defense can't be allowed to disrupt the urgent need to spend on pensions, education, healthcare and infrastructure. "The claim that the country cannot spend more on defense is primarily rooted in domestic politics," Ales Michal, a political scientist at Prague's Charles University, told DW. "The major priority is investment in the social system." That will be welcomed by supporters of the governing parties, who skew older and less well off, and resent the support being given to 300,000 or so Ukrainian refugees . "None of the governing parties promised voters higher defense spending," in campaigning for last year's election, Michal notes. Critics, however, say that's because the government is downplaying the threat from Russia. The government's spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment. 'We don't want World War III' The reticence to raise defense spending also reflects political narratives around the war in Ukraine. Two days after Whitaker's rebuke, Babis appeared in a video dressed in a T-shirt emblazoned with the words "No War" in blue and yellow letters. While he noted the threat from Russia, he called for greater efforts to find peace. "We don't want World War III, do we?" he pronounced, repeating his claim that Europe should work harder to end the conflict. It was a performance echoing the stance of Europe's radical right-wing, and the sort that has seen the Czech PM labelled "pro-Russian" in some international media. The truth is more mundane. Babis is a pragmatist. The ANO electorate is populist and anti-Ukrainian, but also strongly pro-Western. Surveys show that the plan to keep defense spending at 2% of GDP precisely matches its views. Yet Babis's divisive personality leaves the party dependent on extremist partners for enough support to govern, and so he must also try to speak the anti-system, pro-Russian language of the SPD, which, despite controlling the defense ministry, was pushing to cut spending further in the 2027 budget. "A critical stance towards Ukraine also shapes the government's position on spending," said Michal. The pro-peace stance downplaying Russia's aggression moves ANO "closer to the European radical right," he notes, but Babis is "guided by opinion polls," and must try to find a "balance between two polarizing positions." Strategic understanding The opposition sees this dichotomy as the government's Achilles' heel. Martin Kupka, leader of the center-right Civic Democrats (ODS), welcomed Babis's reiterated NATO commitment before asking the PM: "When will you get rid of the Kremlin fifth column, which you took into the government and even entrusted with the Ministry of Defense?" However, although the ODS-led government that held office between 2021 and 2025 offered fervent support to Ukraine, like all its predecessors, it also failed to meet the NATO spending target. "Our partners may be unhappy about the approach to spending, but it's the reality of the political situation in our country," Andor Sandor, a defense analyst and former commander of Czechia's Military Intelligence Service, told DW. However, he added that while weak defense spending growth "is not optimal," the biggest issue is a lack of strategic understanding regarding the military's size and role. Computer-generated: The Pentagon UFOs Mysterious ‘black triangles’ spotted over sensitive US site, new Pentagon UFO files reveal Unidentified object vanished suddenly and silently, anonymous senior military observers claim Richard Luscombe Fri 23 Oct 2026 14.45 EDT Last modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 16.23 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Two senior military observers say they watched a mysterious black triangular object flying at an extraordinarily high speed over a sensitive site in the western US earlier this year, in the latest tranche of reported UFO sightings released on Friday by the Trump administration. The unidentified object showed none of the characteristics of a conventional military aircraft, their report to the defense department said, and it vanished suddenly and silently within seconds, leaving no exhaust trail or other evidence of its existence. The claimed sighting, by anonymous sources with “extensive operational experience working alongside government agencies”, occurred at a location that was redacted in the file made public on Friday. The “unidentified anomalous phenomenon” (UAP), a term that has superseded UFO in military, governmental and scientific circles, resembled a delta-wing drone with a wingspan between nine and 15ft (2.75 to 4.5m), the observers recalled. They calculated its speed at 1,800mph. Similar to hundreds of other reports released by the Pentagon since May as part of Donald Trump’s promise to bring transparency to decades of previously classified or secret documents relating to UFOs, many other details are vague, inconclusive or blacked out altogether. While many previous accounts have been accompanied by real photographs or video footage of apparent sightings, the “black triangles” report features nine identical images of the same unidentified canyon with tiny, trilateral silhouettes crudely added to replicate the movement of the object the observers said they saw. “This does indeed look like little more than a black triangle shape superimposed on a landscape background to illustrate the report. I don’t think it really adds anything substantive to the report itself,” said Greg Eghigian, professor of history and bioethics at Penn State University, and author of the 2024 book After the Flying Saucers Came: A Global History of the UFO Phenomenon. After an early flurry, the Pentagon’s releases in the second Trump administration have become less frequent in recent months, and noticeably thinner since the US president declared in February that he was ordering full disclosure about the government’s knowledge of UFOs and the search for alien life beyond our planet. The move followed allegations aired in Congress in 2023 by a former intelligence official that successive administrations engaged in a cover-up, and that the government had possession of crashed alien spacecraft . Friday’s release contained fewer than 25 text documents, and no videos or images.
